sentences.zh: 序

translations.literal: Preface.
translations.idiomatic: Preface

sentences.zh: 昔在庖犧，觀象察法，以通神明之德，以類天地之情，可以藏往知來，開物成務。

translations.literal: In ancient times, when Baoxi (Fu Xi) observed the celestial patterns and examined their norms, he used them to penetrate the virtue of numinous clarity and to categorize the dispositions of Heaven and Earth; by this means one could store the past in mind and know what was to come, open the myriad things to use, and bring affairs to completion.
translations.idiomatic: Long ago Fu Xi read the patterns above and the constants below, that he might grasp the virtue that shines through the spirits and give form to the temper of Heaven and Earth—so the past could be kept in view and the future divined, the tools of life set in order, and the business of the age carried through.

sentences.zh: 故《易》曰：「天垂象，見吉凶，聖人象之。

translations.literal: Therefore the Classic of Changes says: “Heaven hangs down its images, showing fortune and misfortune, and the sage takes them as his model.”
translations.idiomatic: Hence the Zhou yi: “Heaven displays its signs, revealing good or ill fortune, and the sage patterns himself on them.”

sentences.zh: 」此則觀乎天文以示變者也。

translations.literal: ” This, then, is observing astronomical phenomena in order to display change.
translations.idiomatic: That is what it means to read the lights of the sky as emblems of transformation.

sentences.zh: 《尚書》曰：「天聰明自我民聰明。

translations.literal: The Documents says: “Heaven’s keen hearing and keen sight come from the keen hearing and keen sight of the people.”
translations.idiomatic: The Shang shu puts it this way: “Heaven hears and sees as the people hear and see.”

sentences.zh: 」此則觀乎人文以成化者也。

translations.literal: ” This, then, is observing human culture in order to accomplish transformation.
translations.idiomatic: That is what it means to take human affairs as the mirror in which civilization is perfected.

sentences.zh: 是故政教兆-{於}-人理，祥變應乎天文，得失雖微，罔不昭著。

translations.literal: Therefore omens of government and instruction arise from human order, while prodigies and anomalies answer to astronomical patterns; though gain and loss be subtle, none fails to shine forth clearly.
translations.idiomatic: Policy and moral teaching send their first signals through the order of mankind; wonders in the sky answer them from above. However fine the line between success and failure, nothing is hidden from view.

sentences.zh: 然則三皇邁德，七曜順軌，日月無薄蝕之變，星辰靡錯亂之妖。

translations.literal: Thus under the Three Sovereigns virtue was paramount, the seven luminaries followed their tracks, sun and moon showed no dimming or eclipse, and the stars displayed no portents of disorder.
translations.idiomatic: Under the earliest sage-kings, virtue was all in all: the seven governors of the sky kept their courses, sun and moon knew neither eclipse nor flaw, and the constellations gave no sign of havoc.

sentences.zh: 黃帝創受《河圖》，始明休咎，故其《星傳》尚有存焉。

translations.literal: The Yellow Emperor first received the River Chart and began to clarify good fortune and ill; therefore portions of his Star Monograph still survive.
translations.idiomatic: The Yellow Emperor was the first to receive the River Chart and to read blessing and bane from it; fragments of his star lore still survive.

sentences.zh: 降在髙陽，乃命南正重司天，北正黎司地。

translations.literal: Descending to Gaoyang (Zhuanxu), he then commanded South Rectifier Chong to oversee Heaven and North Rectifier Li to oversee Earth.
translations.idiomatic: Later, under Zhuanxu, he appointed Chong of the south as Rectifier of Heaven and Li of the north as Rectifier of Earth.

sentences.zh: 爰洎帝嚳，亦式序三辰。

translations.literal: Continuing to Emperor Ku, he likewise orderly arranged the three luminaries.
translations.idiomatic: By the time of Emperor Ku the three lights—sun, moon, and stars—were again set in proper sequence.

sentences.zh: 唐虞則羲和繼軌，有夏則昆吾紹德。

translations.literal: Under Tang and Yu, Xi and He continued their predecessors’ tracks; under the Xia, Kunwu continued their virtue.
translations.idiomatic: In the age of Yao and Shun, Xi and He maintained the calendar; under the Xia, Kunwu carried the tradition forward.

sentences.zh: 年代綿邈，文籍靡傳。

translations.literal: The years and generations stretch immeasurably far, and written records have not been transmitted.
translations.idiomatic: The centuries between are lost in mist, and little was written down that has reached us.

sentences.zh: 至-{於}-殷之巫-{咸}-，周之史佚，格言遺記，-{於}-今不朽。

translations.literal: As for the Yin, there was the shaman Xian; under the Zhou there was Scribe Yi; their wise sayings and transmitted records down to the present have not perished.
translations.idiomatic: In Shang we hear of the shaman Xian; in Zhou, of Grand Scribe Yi—gnomic lines and memoranda that still live in quotation today.

sentences.zh: 其諸侯之史，則魯有梓愼，晉有-{卜}-偃，鄭有裨竈，宋有子韋，齊有甘德，楚有唐昧，趙有尹皋，魏有石申夫，皆掌著天文，各論圖驗。

translations.literal: Among the scribes of the feudal states, Lu had Zishen, Jin had Boyan, Zheng had Bicheng, Song had Ziwei, Qi had Gan De, Chu had Tang Mei, Zhao had Yin Gao, and Wei had Shi Shenfu; each presided over writing on astronomy and each discussed charts and verification.
translations.idiomatic: Among the regional courts, Lu claimed Zishen, Jin Boyan, Zheng Bicheng, Song Ziwei, Qi Gan De, Chu Tang Mei, Zhao Yin Gao, and Wei Shi Shenfu—each a house astronomer with his own star charts and proofs.

sentences.zh: 其巫-{咸}-、甘、石之説，-{後}-代所宗。

translations.literal: The doctrines of Xian, Gan, and Shi are what later generations take as authoritative.
translations.idiomatic: Later ages chiefly rely on the systems handed down from Xian, Gan De, and Shi Shen.

sentences.zh: 暴秦燔書，六經殘滅，天官星占，存而不毀。

translations.literal: Violent Qin burned the books; the Six Classics were mutilated, yet the offices of Heaven and star divination survived and were not destroyed.
translations.idiomatic: When the Qin tyrant burned the libraries, the classics were shattered, but calendrical offices and star lore escaped the flames.

sentences.zh: 及漢景武之際，司馬談父子繼爲史官，著《天官書》，以明天人之道。

translations.literal: By the reigns of Han Jingdi and Wudi, Sima Tan and his son succeeded one another as scribes and compiled the “Treatise on Celestial Offices,” to clarify the way of Heaven and man.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperors Jing and Wu of Han, Sima Tan and Sima Qian served in turn as grand scribes and wrote the “Heavenly Offices” treatise, mapping the bond between the sky and human rule.

sentences.zh: 其-{後}-中壘校尉劉向，廣《洪-{範}-》災條，作《皇極論》，以參往之行事。

translations.literal: Thereafter Colonel of the Inner Fortress Liu Xiang expanded the calamity entries of the “Great Plan” in the Documents and composed the “Discourse on the August Ultimate,” to compare them with deeds of the past.
translations.idiomatic: Afterward Liu Xiang, as colonel of the inner bastion, enlarged the omen lists of the Hong fan and framed his “August Ultimate” essay, checking each type against history.

sentences.zh: 及班固敘漢史，馬續述《天文》，而蔡邕、譙周各有撰録，司馬彪采之，以繼前-{志}-。

translations.literal: When Ban Gu arranged the history of the Han, Ma Xu set forth the “Treatise on Astronomy”; Cai Yong and Qiao Zhou each had compilations, which Sima Biao gathered to continue the earlier treatises.
translations.idiomatic: Ban Gu’s Han shu gave the narrative, Ma Xu supplied the astronomical monograph, and Cai Yong and Qiao Zhou added materials that Sima Biao later wove into the standard “Treatise on the Heavens.”

sentences.zh: 今詳衆説，以著-{於}-篇。

translations.literal: Now I have examined the various theories and recorded them in this piece.
translations.idiomatic: Here I sift the competing accounts and set out what is worth keeping.

sentences.zh: 天體

translations.literal: The celestial body.
translations.idiomatic: The form of the heavens

sentences.zh: 古言天者有三家，一曰蓋天，二曰宣夜，三曰渾天。

translations.literal: Those who spoke of Heaven in antiquity belonged to three schools: first Gaitian (“canopy heaven”), second Xuanye (“all-night”), third Huntian (“spherical heaven”).
translations.idiomatic: Ancient writers on the sky fall into three camps: the canopy model, the “midnight” void theory, and the armillary-sphere cosmology.

sentences.zh: 漢靈帝時，蔡邕-{于}-朔方上書，言「宣夜之學，絶無師法。

translations.literal: In the time of Han Lingdi, Cai Yong, from his exile in Shuofang, submitted a memorial saying, “The learning of Xuanye has absolutely no transmitted method.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor Ling of Han, Cai Yong wrote from Shuofang that the Xuanye school had no living line of teachers or texts.

sentences.zh: 《周髀》-{術}-數具存，考驗天狀，多所違失。

translations.literal: The Zhou bi’s computations survive intact, yet when tested against the actual state of Heaven they often contradict and miss.
translations.idiomatic: The Zhou bi arithmetic is still there, but when you hold it against observation it fails in many places.

sentences.zh: 惟渾天近得其情，今史官候-{台}-所用銅儀則其法也。

translations.literal: Only Huntian nearly captures the reality; the bronze instruments used today by the clerks on the observatory platform follow its method.
translations.idiomatic: Only the Huntian scheme comes close to the facts; the bronze armillary in the observatory today is built on that design.

sentences.zh: 立八尺圓體而具天地之形，以正黃道，占察-{發}-斂，以行日月，以歩五緯，精微深妙，百代不易之道也。

translations.literal: They erect an eight-foot sphere showing the forms of Heaven and Earth, to align the Yellow Road, to observe waxing and waning, to move the sun and moon, and to pace the five planets—subtle, profound, and subtle, a Way unchanged through a hundred generations.
translations.idiomatic: An eight-foot globe models both spheres, fixes the ecliptic, tracks the seasons, carries sun and moon, and steps the five wanderers—a fine, durable system that has not gone out of date.

sentences.zh: 官有其器而無本書，前-{志}-亦闕」。

translations.literal: The office has the instruments but lacks the basic texts, and the earlier treatises are likewise incomplete.”
translations.idiomatic: Yet the bureau owns the hardware without the old manuals, and earlier histories left gaps as well.”

sentences.zh: 蔡邕所謂《周髀》者，即蓋天之説也。

translations.literal: What Cai Yong called the Zhou bi is the theory of Gaitian.
translations.idiomatic: Cai Yong’s “Zhou bi” is simply another name for the canopy-heaven school.

sentences.zh: 其本庖犧氏立周天暦度，其所傳則周公受-{于}-殷商，周人-{志}-之，故曰《周髀》。

translations.literal: Its origin is that the clan of Baoxi established the degrees of the round Heaven calendar; what it transmits is that the Duke of Zhou received it from Yin-Shang, and the Zhou people recorded it, hence it is called Zhou bi.
translations.idiomatic: Tradition traces it to Fu Xi’s measurement of the circular sky; the Duke of Zhou is said to have received the method from Shang, and the Zhou scribes wrote it into the Zhou bi.

sentences.zh: 髀，股也；

translations.literal: Bi means “thigh.”
translations.idiomatic: Bi here means the thigh.

sentences.zh: 股者，表也。

translations.literal: “Thigh” means the gnomon.
translations.idiomatic: In this usage it is the vertical rod—the gnomon.

sentences.zh: 其言天似蓋笠，地法覆槃，天地各中髙外下。

translations.literal: It says Heaven is like an upturned bamboo hat and Earth like an inverted basin; Heaven and Earth are each higher in the center and lower at the rim.
translations.idiomatic: The model pictures heaven as a sun-hat and earth as an upside-down bowl, each domed toward the middle.

sentences.zh: 北極之下爲天地之中，其地最髙，而滂沲四隤，三光隱映，以爲晝夜。

translations.literal: Beneath the north pole is the center of Heaven and Earth; that land is the highest, and on four sides it spreads and slopes downward; the three luminaries hide and shine therein, thereby making day and night.
translations.idiomatic: Under the pole lies the pivot of the world, the highest ground; the terrain falls away on every side while sun, moon, and stars wheel overhead to make light and dark.

sentences.zh: 天中髙-{於}-外衡冬至日之所在六萬-{里}-，北極下地髙-{於}-外衡下地亦六萬-{里}-，外衡髙-{於}-北極下地二萬-{里}-。

translations.literal: The height of heaven’s center above the outer cord where the winter solstice sun resides is sixty thousand li; the height of the pole above the ground beneath the outer cord is likewise sixty thousand li; the outer cord is twenty thousand li higher than the ground beneath the north pole.
translations.idiomatic: Their geometry puts the zenith sixty thousand li above the winter-solstice circle, the pole the same height above the horizon there, and the outer winter track twenty thousand li above the polar plain.

sentences.zh: 天地隆髙相從，日去地恆八萬-{里}-。

translations.literal: Heaven and earth’s heights correspond; the sun is constantly eighty thousand li from the earth.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven and earth stay in proportion, and the sun keeps a fixed eighty-thousand-li standoff from the ground.

sentences.zh: 日麗天而平轉，分冬夏之間日所行道爲七衡六間。

translations.literal: The sun clings to heaven and rotates on the level; they divide the path the sun travels between winter and summer into seven cords and six intervals.
translations.idiomatic: The sun rides the turning sky; its annual track is marked out as seven “balances” and the six gaps between them.

sentences.zh: 毎衡周徑-{里}-數，各依算-{術}-，用句股重差推晷影極-{遊}-，以爲遠近之數，皆得-{於}-表股者也。

translations.literal: For each cord’s circumference and diameter in li, each follows computational methods; using gou-gu and double difference they push the extremes of gnomon shadow travel to obtain numbers of near and far—all obtained from gnomon and thigh.
translations.idiomatic: Each ring’s size is derived by right-triangle math and double differencing of solstice shadows—hence the work’s name, “Zhou bi,” the Zhou gnomon.

sentences.zh: 故曰《周髀》。

translations.literal: Therefore it is called Zhou bi.
translations.idiomatic: That is why the treatise bears the title Zhou bi.

sentences.zh: 又《周髀》家-{云}-：「天圓如張蓋，地方如棋局。

translations.literal: Again the Zhou bi school says: “Heaven is round like a stretched canopy, earth is square like a chessboard.
translations.idiomatic: The school also says: “The sky is a round umbrella, the land a flat chessboard.”

sentences.zh: 天旁轉如推磨而左行，日月右行，隨天左轉，故日月實東行，而天牽之以西沒。

translations.literal: Heaven turns at the rim like a millstone turning left, while the sun and moon move right, following heaven’s leftward rotation; therefore the sun and moon really move eastward, but heaven drags them so that they sink in the west.
translations.idiomatic: The dome spins counterclockwise like a mill; the luminaries slip clockwise along it, so they actually crawl eastward yet seem dragged westward into night.

sentences.zh: 譬之-{於}-蟻行磨石之上，磨左旋而蟻右去，磨疾而蟻遲，故不得不隨磨以左回焉。

translations.literal: Compare it to an ant walking on a grindstone: the mill turns left while the ant goes right; the mill is fast and the ant slow, so the ant cannot but follow the mill and turn left.
translations.idiomatic: Think of an ant on a turning quern: the stone whirls one way, the insect treads the other, yet the net motion follows the wheel.

sentences.zh: 天形南髙而北下，日出髙，故見；

translations.literal: Heaven’s form is higher in the south and lower in the north; the sun emerges high, therefore it is visible;
translations.idiomatic: Because the canopy tilts, the south lifts the sun into view;

sentences.zh: 日入下，故不見。

translations.literal: the sun enters low, therefore it is not visible.
translations.idiomatic: while the lowered north lets it slip from sight.

sentences.zh: 天之居如倚蓋，故極在人北，是其證也。

translations.literal: Heaven’s position is like a leaning canopy; therefore the pole is north of mankind—this is the proof.
translations.idiomatic: The axis stands north of us like the pole of a tilted parasol—proof of the model.

sentences.zh: 極在天之中，而今在人北，所以知天之形如倚蓋也。

translations.literal: The pole is at heaven’s center, yet now it is north of mankind; hence one knows heaven’s form is like a leaning canopy.
translations.idiomatic: The celestial pivot should be dead overhead, yet we see it in the north; only a sloping sky explains that.

sentences.zh: 日朝出陽中，暮入陰中，陰氣暗冥，故沒不見也。

translations.literal: At dawn the sun emerges in the midst of yang; at dusk it enters the midst of yin; yin qi is dark, therefore it sets and is not seen.
translations.idiomatic: Dawn lifts the sun into the bright yang quarter; dusk drops it into murky yin, where light dies away.

sentences.zh: 夏時陽氣多，陰氣少，陽氣光明，與日同輝，故日出即見，無蔽之者，故夏日長也。

translations.literal: In summer yang qi is abundant and yin qi scant; yang qi is bright and shares radiance with the sun, therefore as soon as the sun emerges it is seen, with nothing to screen it; hence summer days are long.
translations.idiomatic: Summer air is mostly yang, clear as the disk itself, so sunrise brings instant daylight and the hours stretch.

sentences.zh: 冬天陰氣多，陽氣少，陰氣暗冥，掩日之光，雖出猶隱不見，故冬日短也。」

translations.literal: In winter yin qi is abundant and yang qi scant; yin qi is dark and veils the sun’s light; though it emerges it still hides and is not seen; hence winter days are short.”
translations.idiomatic: Winter is thick with yin haze that masks the orb; even at noon the sun seems shy, and the daylight hours shrink.”

sentences.zh: 宣夜之書亡，惟漢秘書郎郗萌記先師相傳-{云}-：「天了無質，仰而瞻之，髙遠無極，眼瞀精絶，故蒼蒼然也。

translations.literal: The books of Xuanye are lost; only the Han secretary Xi Meng recorded what his masters transmitted, saying: “Heaven altogether lacks substance; gazing upward, its height runs out into the boundless; the eyes are dazzled and the vital force exhausted, hence it appears deep blue.
translations.idiomatic: Xuanye’s texts are gone; Xi Meng of the Han secretariat preserved a teacher’s dictum: the sky is not a solid shell—stare upward and it goes on forever until the eye fails, leaving only a wash of blue.

sentences.zh: 譬之旁望遠道之黃山而皆靑，俯察千仞之深-{谷}-而窈黑，夫靑非眞色，而黑非有體也。

translations.literal: Compare it to looking sideways along a distant yellow mountain and seeing it all as green, or peering down a thousand-ren deep valley and seeing black-green; the green is not a true color, nor does the black possess substance.
translations.idiomatic: It is like misty peaks turning blue in distance or a gorge reading as black—color borrowed from air, not pigment.

sentences.zh: 日月衆星，自然浮生虚空之中，其行其止皆須氣焉。

translations.literal: The sun, moon, and host of stars float by nature in empty void; their moving and stopping all depend on qi.
translations.idiomatic: Sun, moon, and stars drift in the void, their motion and rest wholly governed by the pneuma that fills space.

sentences.zh: 是以七曜或逝或住，或順或逆，伏見無常，進退不同，由乎無所根-{系}-，故各異也。

translations.literal: Therefore the seven luminaries sometimes depart and sometimes rest, sometimes go with and sometimes against the grain, hidden and visible without constancy, advancing and retreating unlike one another—because they have nothing to which they are tied, each differs.
translations.idiomatic: Hence the seven governors race, idle, advance, retreat, hide, and shine on no fixed schedule: nothing ties them to a single track.

sentences.zh: 故辰極常居其所，而北-{斗}-不與衆星西沒也。

translations.literal: Therefore the pole of time regularly stays in its place, while the Northern Dipper does not sink in the west together with the other stars.
translations.idiomatic: The pole stays put while the Dipper does not share the common westward set of the constellations.

sentences.zh: 攝提、塡星皆東行，日行一度，月行十三度，遲疾任情，其無所-{系}-著可知矣。

translations.literal: Sheti, Saturn, all move eastward; the sun moves one du per day, the moon thirteen du, slow and fast at whim—their having nothing to fix them to is knowable.
translations.idiomatic: Jupiter’s station, Saturn, and the rest drift east at their own rates—one degree a day for the sun, thirteen for the moon—showing plainly that nothing pegs them to a rigid wheel.

sentences.zh: 若綴附天體，不得爾也。

translations.literal: If they were hung upon the celestial body, it could not be so.
translations.idiomatic: Were they nailed to a turning sphere, they could not behave like this.

sentences.zh: 成帝-{咸}-康中，會稽虞喜因宣夜之説作《安天論》，以爲「天髙窮-{於}-無窮，地深測-{於}-不測。

translations.literal: In Chengdi’s Xianning years, Kuaiji Yu Xi, following Xuanye’s theory, composed the “Secure Heaven Treatise,” holding that “Heaven’s height runs out into the boundless, earth’s depth measures into the unfathomable.
translations.idiomatic: Under Jin Chengdi’s Xianning era (335–342), Yu Xi of Kuaiji reworked Xuanye into an “Anchored Sky” essay: height without limit above, depth without floor below.

sentences.zh: 天確乎在上，有常安之形；

translations.literal: Heaven is truly above, with a form of constant stillness;
translations.idiomatic: Heaven stays aloft in changeless calm;

sentences.zh: 地塊焉在下，有居靜之體。

translations.literal: earth is a clod below, with a substance of quiet rest.
translations.idiomatic: earth rests below as a settled clod.

sentences.zh: 當相覆冒，方則倶方，圓則倶圓，無方圓不同之義也。

translations.literal: When they cover each other, if square then both are square, if round then both are round; there is no meaning of round and square being different.
translations.idiomatic: If one is square the other must be square; if round, both round—no mismatch of shapes.

sentences.zh: 其光曜布列，各自運行，猶江海之有潮汐，萬品之有行藏也」。

translations.literal: Their light radiance spreading in array each moves on its own, like the tides of rivers and seas, like the going and hiding of the myriad kinds.”
translations.idiomatic: Lights in the firmament move as freely as tides or creatures showing and hiding at will.”

sentences.zh: 葛洪聞而譏之曰：「苟辰宿不麗-{於}-天，天爲無用，便可言無，何必-{復}--{雲}-有之而不動乎？

translations.literal: Ge Hong heard this and ridiculed it, saying: “If the star lodges are not attached to heaven, heaven would be useless; one might simply say it does not exist—why must you again say there is something that does not move?
translations.idiomatic: Ge Hong mocked him: “If constellations do not ride the sky, the sky is otiose—you might as well call it nothing. Why insist on a heaven that neither moves nor matters?”

sentences.zh: 」由此而談，稚川可謂知言之選也。

translations.literal: ” From this point of view, Zhichuan may be called a chooser of discerning words.
translations.idiomatic: On this score Zhichuan shows a critic’s ear.

sentences.zh: 虞喜族祖河間相聳又立穹天論-{云}-：「天形穹隆如鷄子，幕其際，周接四海之表，浮-{於}-元氣之上。

translations.literal: Yu Xi’s clansman-by-generation, Hejian Chancellor Song, again set forth the “Arc Heaven Treatise,” saying: “Heaven’s shape is domed like an egg; where it meets the rim it joins the surface of the four seas, floating on primordial qi above.
translations.idiomatic: Yu Song, Yu Xi’s kinsman and chancellor of Hejian, proposed a “Domed Sky”: the firmament is an eggshell meeting the ocean at the rim, buoyed on primordial vapor.

sentences.zh: 譬如覆奩以抑水，而不沒者，氣充其中故也。

translations.literal: It is like turning a covered mirror over on water yet it does not sink—because qi fills within.
translations.idiomatic: Like a cup pressed mouth-down on a pond yet held up by the air locked inside.

sentences.zh: 日繞辰極，沒西而還東，不出入地中。

translations.literal: The sun circles the pole of time, sets in the west and returns east, not entering and emerging from within the earth.
translations.idiomatic: The sun wheels about the pole, vanishing in the west and reappearing in the east, never tunneling underfoot.

sentences.zh: 天之有極，猶蓋之有-{斗}-也。

translations.literal: Heaven’s having a pole is like a canopy’s having a pivot.
translations.idiomatic: A pivot for the sky matches the hub that holds a parasol.

sentences.zh: 天北下-{於}-地三十度，極之傾在地卯酉之北亦三十度，人在卯酉之南十-{餘}-萬-{里}-，故-{斗}-極之下不爲地中，當對天地卯酉之位耳。

translations.literal: Heaven is thirty degrees lower than earth toward the north; the pole’s tilt north of the mao-you line on earth is likewise thirty degrees; mankind is more than a hundred thousand li south of mao-you; therefore beneath the Dipper and pole is not earth’s center but faces the mao-you position of heaven and earth.
translations.idiomatic: He tilts the axis thirty degrees north of the east–west belt while mankind sits more than a hundred thousand li south of that belt, so the subpolar point is not the world’s middle but the spot where heaven’s and earth’s east–west lines cross.

sentences.zh: 日行黃道繞極，極北去黃道百一十五度，南去黃道六十七度，二至之所-{舍}-以爲長短也。」

translations.literal: The sun’s path is the Yellow Road circling the pole; the pole is one hundred fifteen du north of the Yellow Road and sixty-seven du south of the Yellow Road; the lodges where the two solstices reside determine length.”
translations.idiomatic: The ecliptic girdles the pole, which lies 115° north of the ring at one limit and 67° south at the other; where summer and winter pause sets the scale of long and short days.”

sentences.zh: 呉太常姚信造昕天論-{云}-：「人爲靈-{蟲}-，形最似天。

translations.literal: Wu’s Minister of the Imperial Clan Yao Xin composed the “Dawn Heaven Treatise,” saying: “Man is the numinous insect; his form most resembles heaven.
translations.idiomatic: Yao Xin, Wu’s minister for the imperial clan, wrote the “Heaven at Sunrise” piece: humanity is the wise creature whose body best mirrors the sky.

sentences.zh: 今人頤前侈臨胸，而項不能覆背。

translations.literal: Now a man’s chin front bulges forward toward the chest, while the nape cannot cover the back.
translations.idiomatic: Our faces lean south over the breast while the neck cannot hood the back—an anatomy lesson.

sentences.zh: 近取諸身，故知天之體南低入地，北則偏髙。

translations.literal: Taking analogy from what is near in one’s body, one therefore knows heaven’s body is low entering the earth on the south, while on the north it is inclined high.
translations.idiomatic: By that likeness we infer a southern rim plunging toward the ground and a northern canopy lifted high.

sentences.zh: 又冬至極低，而天運近南，故日去人遠，而-{斗}-去人近，北天氣至，故冰寒也。

translations.literal: Again, at winter solstice the pole is lowest and heaven’s motion is nearest the south, therefore the sun is far from people while the Dipper is near; northern heaven’s qi arrives, hence ice and cold.
translations.idiomatic: At winter solstice the axis dips, the machinery hugs the south, the sun stands far off while the Dipper crowds overhead, and northern cold pours in.

sentences.zh: 夏至極起，而天運近北，故-{斗}-去人遠，日去人近，南天氣至，故蒸熱也。

translations.literal: At summer solstice the pole rises and heaven’s motion is nearest the north, therefore the Dipper is far from people and the sun is near; southern heaven’s qi arrives, hence steaming heat.
translations.idiomatic: At summer solstice the pole lifts, motion hugs the north, the Dipper recedes, the sun draws close, and southern heat swamps us.

sentences.zh: 極之立時，日行地中淺，故夜短；

translations.literal: When the pole stands high, the sun runs shallowly within the earth, hence the night is short;
translations.idiomatic: When the pole rides high, the sun’s underworld path is shallow, so nights are brief;

sentences.zh: 天去地髙，故晝長也。

translations.literal: heaven is far from earth, hence the day is long.
translations.idiomatic: the sky arches far above, so days are long.

sentences.zh: 極之低時，日行地中深，故夜長；

translations.literal: When the pole is low, the sun runs deep within the earth, hence the night is long;
translations.idiomatic: When the pole hangs low, the sun dives deep, stretching night;

sentences.zh: 天去地下，故晝短也。」

translations.literal: heaven is close to earth below, hence the day is short.”
translations.idiomatic: the canopy presses near, shortening daylight.”

sentences.zh: 自虞喜、虞聳、姚信皆好奇徇異之説，非極數談天者也。

translations.literal: From Yu Xi, Yu Song, and Yao Xin onward, all are theories that favor novelty and pursue the strange; they are not those who exhaust numbers to discourse on Heaven.
translations.idiomatic: Yu Xi, Yu Song, and Yao Xin traded in clever paradox, not in the patient reckoning true astronomy demands.

sentences.zh: 至-{於}-渾天理妙，學者多疑。

translations.literal: As for Huntian’s principle being subtle, scholars mostly doubt it.
translations.idiomatic: The armillary-sphere doctrine is subtle, and most scholars hesitate before it.

sentences.zh: 漢王仲任據蓋天之説，以駁渾儀-{云}-：「舊説天轉從地下過。

translations.literal: Han’s Wang Chong, relying on Gaitian theory, refuted the armillary instrument, saying: “The old theory says heaven turns passing beneath the ground.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Chong of Han, a canopy partisan, attacked the sphere: “The old tale says the sky wheels beneath us.

sentences.zh: 今掘地一丈輒有水，天何得從水中行乎？

translations.literal: Now dig the ground one zhang and there is always water; how could heaven pass traveling within water?
translations.idiomatic: Dig a few feet and you strike water—how does the firmament swim through a global ocean?”

sentences.zh: 甚不然也。

translations.literal: It is utterly not so.
translations.idiomatic: That cannot be right.

sentences.zh: 日隨天而轉，非入地。

translations.literal: The sun follows heaven and turns; it does not enter the earth.
translations.idiomatic: The sun rides the turning sky; it never bores into the soil.

sentences.zh: 夫有目所望，不過十-{里}-，天地合矣；

translations.literal: What the eye can see extends no more than ten li, then heaven and earth merge;
translations.idiomatic: Sight fails within ten li, so horizon and sky seem to meet;

sentences.zh: 實非合也，遠使然耳。

translations.literal: in fact they do not merge; distance makes it seem so.
translations.idiomatic: they do not truly touch; distance tricks the eye.

sentences.zh: 今視日入，非入也，亦遠耳。

translations.literal: Now when we see the sun set, it is not entering; again it is distance.
translations.idiomatic: So too sunset: not immersion, only remoteness.

sentences.zh: 當日入西方之時，其下之人亦將謂之爲中也。

translations.literal: When the sun is setting in the west, the people thereunder will likewise take it to be at the zenith.
translations.idiomatic: To watchers westward, that sinking orb stands at their zenith.

sentences.zh: 四方之人，各以其所近者爲出，遠者爲入矣。

translations.literal: People of the four quarters each take what is near them as emergence and what is distant as entering.
translations.idiomatic: Each quarter calls its own horizon “rise” and the far rim “set.”

sentences.zh: 何以明之？

translations.literal: How is it proved?
translations.idiomatic: How show it?

sentences.zh: 今試使一人把大炬火，夜行-{於}-平地，去人十-{里}-，火光滅矣；

translations.literal: Now try to have someone carry a great torch walking by night on level ground; at ten li from people the fire’s light is gone;
translations.idiomatic: Send a man with a blazing brand across a plain: ten li off the flame disappears from view;

sentences.zh: 非滅也。

translations.literal: it is not gone.
translations.idiomatic: the torch still burns.

sentences.zh: 遠使然耳。

translations.literal: Distance makes it seem so.
translations.idiomatic: Distance merely hides it.

sentences.zh: 今日西轉不-{復}-見，是火滅之類也。

translations.literal: Now the sun turning west and no longer being seen belongs to the category of the fire going out.
translations.idiomatic: So with the westering sun—extinction is only appearance.

sentences.zh: 日月不員也，望視之所從員者，去人遠也。

translations.literal: The sun and moon are not round; what makes what gazing from afar follows round is that they are far from people.
translations.idiomatic: They need not be perfect spheres; distance rounds every disk.

sentences.zh: 夫日，火之精也；

translations.literal: The sun is the essence of fire;
translations.idiomatic: The sun is fire refined;

sentences.zh: 月，水之精也。

translations.literal: the moon is the essence of water.
translations.idiomatic: the moon, water refined.

sentences.zh: 水火在地下員，在天何故員？

translations.literal: Water and fire on the ground form round shapes; why, when in the heavens, should they be round?
translations.idiomatic: Fire and water on earth make rounded pools of flame and dew—why insist the sky’s copies must be geometric globes?

sentences.zh: 」故丹陽葛洪釋之曰：《渾天儀注》-{云}-：「天如鷄子，地如鷄中黃，孤居-{於}-天内，天大而地小。

translations.literal: ” Therefore Danyang Ge Hong explained: The “Huntian Instrument Commentary” says: “Heaven is like an egg white, earth is like the yolk inside the egg, solitary residing within heaven; heaven is large and earth small.
translations.idiomatic: ” Ge Hong of Danyang answered with the Huntian gloss: heaven is the shell, earth the yolk adrift within—vast sky, tiny globe.

sentences.zh: 天表-{裏}-有水，天地各乘氣而立，載水而行。

translations.literal: There is water inside and outside heaven’s shell; heaven and earth each stand supported on qi and move riding on water.
translations.idiomatic: Water lines the inner and outer shell; both spheres ride vapor and sail that dark sea.

sentences.zh: 周天三百六十五度四分度之一，又中分之，則半覆地上，半繞地下，故二十八宿半見半隱，天轉如車轂之運也。

translations.literal: The round of Heaven is three hundred sixty-five and one-quarter du; again halving it, then half covers the ground above and half winds beneath the ground below; therefore the twenty-eight lodges are half seen and half hidden, and Heaven turns like the hub of a cart wheel in motion.
translations.idiomatic: The celestial circle runs 365¼ degrees; half rides above us and half below, which is why the twenty-eight mansions are half visible and half hidden as the sky wheels like a chariot nave.

sentences.zh: 」諸論天者雖多，然精-{於}-陰陽者少。

translations.literal: ” Though those who discourse on Heaven are many, those who are adept in yin-yang are few.
translations.idiomatic: ” Many have theories of the sky; few truly master yin and yang.

sentences.zh: 張平子、陸公紀之徒，-{咸}-以爲推歩七曜之道，以度暦象昏明之證候，校以四八之氣，考以漏刻之分，占晷景之往來，求形驗-{于}-事情，莫密-{於}-渾象者也。

translations.literal: Men such as Zhang Pingzi and Lu Gongji all held that for pacing the seven luminaries, for using measures and calendar signs to verify dusk and dawn, for checking against the qi of the four seasons and eight nodes, for examining clepsydra divisions, for divining the comings and goings of gnomon shadows, and for seeking shape and verification in actual affairs, nothing is more exact than the armillary sphere.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Heng, Lu Ji, and their school argued that to track the seven governors, time dusk and dawn against the ephemeris, test the solstices and nodes, read the water-clock, and match shadows to facts, nothing beats a bronze armillary.

sentences.zh: 張平子既作銅渾天儀，-{於}-密室中以漏水轉之，令伺之者閉戸而唱之。

translations.literal: After Zhang Pingzi had cast the bronze armillary sphere, in a sealed chamber he turned it with dripping water, ordering the observer to close the door and call out the positions.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Heng set his bronze universe in a dark room, driven by a clepsydra, while an attendant behind closed doors called out each transit.

sentences.zh: 其伺之者以告靈-{台}-之觀天者曰：「璿璣所加，某星始見，某星已中，某星今沒」，皆如合符也。

translations.literal: The observer reported to the Lingtai astronomers: “At the such-and-such mark of the armillary, such-and-such a star first appears, such-and-such a star is now at the meridian, such-and-such a star is now setting”—all matching tally slips.
translations.idiomatic: His cry matched the bureau’s log: “At this pivot angle, that star rises, this one culminates, that one sets”—every call checked like a tally split in two.

sentences.zh: 崔子玉爲其碑銘曰：「數-{術}-窮天地，-{製}-作侔造化，髙-{才}-偉藝，與神合契。

translations.literal: Cui Ziyu wrote for him an inscription on the stele: “His computations exhaust Heaven and Earth; his creations rival transformation itself; lofty talent and great craft join in covenant with the spirits.”
translations.idiomatic: Cui Yin’s stele text runs: “His numbers span heaven and earth; his engines rival nature’s own—genius and art sealed with the divine.”

sentences.zh: 」蓋由-{於}-平子渾儀及地動儀之有驗故也。

translations.literal: ” This was because Pingzi’s armillary and seismoscope had been verified.
translations.idiomatic: ” Small wonder, after the armillary and the earthquake instrument proved themselves in use.

sentences.zh: 若天果如渾者，則天之出入行-{于}-水中，爲的然矣。

translations.literal: If Heaven is truly as the Huntian model, then Heaven’s emerging and entering moving on water is indeed certain.
translations.idiomatic: If the egg-shell cosmos is right, the sky really does pass through the waters—plainly so.

sentences.zh: 故黃帝書曰，「天在地外，水在天外」，水浮天而載地者也。

translations.literal: Therefore the Yellow Emperor’s book says, “Heaven is outside the earth, water is outside Heaven”—water floats Heaven and bears Earth.
translations.idiomatic: A Yellow Emperor text says heaven wraps earth and water wraps heaven—the ocean buoys the firmament and carries the globe.

sentences.zh: 又《易》曰：「時乘六龍。

translations.literal: Again the Changes says: “At the proper times he rides the six dragons.”
translations.idiomatic: The Zhou yi adds: “He mounts the six dragons in season.”

sentences.zh: 」夫陽爻稱龍，龍者居水之物，以喩天。

translations.literal: ” The yang lines are called dragons; the dragon is a creature that dwells in water, used as a metaphor for Heaven.
translations.idiomatic: ” Yang lines are named “dragon,” and dragons live in water—hence the image for heaven.

sentences.zh: 天，陽物也，又出入水中，與龍相似，故以比龍也。

translations.literal: Heaven is a yang entity; moreover it emerges and enters within water, resembling the dragon; therefore it is compared to the dragon.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven is yang; like a dragon it slips into and out of the deep—so the classic pairs them.

sentences.zh: 聖人仰觀俯察，審其如此，故《晉》卦《坤》下《離》上，以證日出-{於}-地也。

translations.literal: The sage looked up and looked down, examined that it was so; therefore the hexagram Jin has Kun below and Li above, to verify the sun emerging from the earth.
translations.idiomatic: The sages read heaven and earth and set the Jin hexagram—earth below, fire above—to show the sun climbing from under the horizon.

sentences.zh: 又《明夷》之卦《離》下《坤》上，以證日入-{於}-地也。

translations.literal: Again the hexagram Ming yi has Li below and Kun above, to verify the sun entering into the earth.
translations.idiomatic: Ming yi reverses the stack—fire under earth—to picture sunset swallowed by the ground.

sentences.zh: 《需》卦《-{乾}-》下《坎》上，此亦天入水中之象也。

translations.literal: The hexagram Xu has Qian below and Kan above; this too is an image of Heaven entering the water.
translations.idiomatic: The Xu hexagram pairs heaven above surging water—another emblem of the sky wading through the flood.

sentences.zh: 天爲金，金水相生之物也。

translations.literal: Heaven is metal; metal and water are things that mutually engender.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven belongs to metal in the cycle, and metal begets water.

sentences.zh: 天出入水中，當有何損，而謂爲不可乎？

translations.literal: Heaven emerging and entering within water—what harm could there be in that, that one should call it impossible?
translations.idiomatic: What injury is there if heaven dips through the sea? Why call it impossible?

sentences.zh: 故桓君山曰：「春分日出卯入酉，此乃人之卯酉。

translations.literal: Therefore Lord Huan Shan said: “At spring equinox the sun emerges in mao and enters you—this is mankind’s mao and you.
translations.idiomatic: Huan Tan observed: “At spring equinox the sun rises in east mao and sets in west you—for us, that is our east–west line.”

sentences.zh: 天之卯酉，常値-{斗}-極爲天中。

translations.literal: Heaven’s mao and you constantly take the Dipper’s pole as the center of Heaven.
translations.idiomatic: For the sky itself, east and west pivot on the celestial pole.

sentences.zh: 今視之乃在北，不正在人上。

translations.literal: Now when we look, it is in the north, not directly above people.
translations.idiomatic: Yet we see that pivot in the north, not overhead.

sentences.zh: 而春秋分時，日出入乃在-{斗}-極之南。

translations.literal: Yet at spring and autumn equinox, the sun’s emergence and entry is south of the Dipper’s pole.
translations.idiomatic: At the equinoxes the sun still rises and sets south of the pole.

sentences.zh: 若如磨右轉，則北方道遠而南方道近，晝夜漏刻之數不應等也。

translations.literal: If it were like a mill turning right, then the northern path would be far and the southern path near, and the numbers of day and night clepsydra divisions ought not be equal.
translations.idiomatic: Were the canopy a millstone spun clockwise, the northern arc would be longer than the southern and day and night would not balance at equinox.

sentences.zh: 」-{後}-奏事待報，坐西廊廡下，以寒故暴背。

translations.literal: ” Later, when presenting a memorial and awaiting a reply, he sat under the western gallery; because of the cold he bared his back to the sun.
translations.idiomatic: ” Later, waiting on business in the western cloister, he sunned his back against the chill.

sentences.zh: 有頃，日光出去，不-{復}-暴背。

translations.literal: After a while the sunlight moved away and he could no longer sun his back.
translations.idiomatic: Presently the beam slid off and the warmth failed.

sentences.zh: 君山乃告信蓋天者曰：「天若如推磨右轉而日西行者，其可知矣。

translations.literal: Lord Shan then told a believer in Gaitian: “If Heaven is like a mill turning right while the sun moves west, that can be understood.
translations.idiomatic: He turned to a canopy partisan: “If the sky were a millwheel and the sun walked west, we could reason it out.

sentences.zh: 」然則天出入水中，無-{復}-疑矣。

translations.literal: ” Then Heaven’s emerging and entering within water is without further doubt.
translations.idiomatic: ” In that case heaven’s passage through water would be certain—but watch what the sunbeam did.”

sentences.zh: 又今視諸星出-{於}-東者，初但去地小許耳。

translations.literal: Again, now when we watch the various stars that emerge in the east, at first they are only a little distance from the ground.
translations.idiomatic: Watch eastern stars at first lift: they hug the horizon.

sentences.zh: 漸而西行，先經人上，從遂西轉而下焉，不旁旋也。

translations.literal: Gradually they move westward, first passing above people, then following by turning west and downward, not wheeling sideways.
translations.idiomatic: They climb overhead, then sink straight west—never skirting the northern rim in a loop.

sentences.zh: 其先在西之星，亦稍下而沒，無北轉者。

translations.literal: Those stars that were first in the west likewise sink slightly and set, with none turning north.
translations.idiomatic: Western stars likewise slip down to set without a northern detour.

sentences.zh: 日之出入亦然。

translations.literal: The sun’s emergence and entry is likewise.
translations.idiomatic: The sun behaves the same way.

sentences.zh: 若謂天磨右轉者，日之出入亦然，衆日月宜隨夫而回，初在-{於}-東，次經-{于}-南，次到-{於}-西，次及-{於}-北，而-{復}-還-{於}-東，不應橫過去也。

translations.literal: If one says Heaven is a mill turning right, the sun’s emergence and entry ought likewise to be so; the sun and moon ought to follow it and wheel back, first in the east, next passing the south, next arriving in the west, next reaching the north, and again returning to the east; they ought not to cross transversely.
translations.idiomatic: If the sky were a clockwise mill, the luminaries should orbit east–south–west–north in order; they should not slice straight across.

sentences.zh: 今日出-{於}-東，冉冉轉上，及其入西，亦-{復}-漸漸稍下，都不繞邊北去。

translations.literal: Now the sun emerges in the east, slowly turning upward; when it reaches its entry in the west, again it gradually sinks slightly downward, in no case winding northward along the rim.
translations.idiomatic: Instead the sun eases up from the east and eases down in the west, never hugging the northern edge.

sentences.zh: 了了如此，王生必固謂爲不然者，疎矣。

translations.literal: It is clear as this; if Master Wang must stubbornly say it is not so, he is obtuse.
translations.idiomatic: The facts are plain; for Wang Chong to dig in his heels is simply perverse.

sentences.zh: 今日徑千-{里}-，圍周三千-{里}-，中足以當小星之數十也。

translations.literal: Now the sun’s diameter is a thousand li, its circumference three thousand li—within it there is enough to match several tens of small stars.
translations.idiomatic: The sun spans a thousand li across and three thousand around—room inside for dozens of lesser stars.

sentences.zh: 若日以轉遠之故，但當光曜不能-{復}-來照及人耳，宜猶望見其體，不應都失其所在也。

translations.literal: If because the sun turns far away its radiance ought no longer to reach and illumine people, one ought still to be able to see its body; it ought not entirely to lose its location.
translations.idiomatic: If distance alone dimmed it, we should still see the disk; it should not vanish without trace.

sentences.zh: 日光既盛，其體又大-{於}-星多矣。

translations.literal: The sun’s light is already brilliant, and its body is also much larger than stars.
translations.idiomatic: The sun outshines and outsizes any star many times over.

sentences.zh: 今見極北之小星，而不見日之在北者，明其不北行也。

translations.literal: Now we see the small stars in the extreme north yet do not see the sun when it is in the north—this makes clear that it does not travel north.
translations.idiomatic: We can spot faint polar stars but never a northern sun—proof it does not wheel north.

sentences.zh: 若日以轉還之故，不-{復}-可見，其北入之間，應當稍小，而日方入之時乃更大，此非轉遠之-{-{徴}-}-也。

translations.literal: If because the sun turns and returns it ought no longer to be visible, in the interval of its northern entry it ought gradually to become smaller; yet when the sun is just entering it becomes larger—this is not the sign of turning farther away.
translations.idiomatic: If recession hid it, the disk should shrink as it dipped north; at sunset it swells instead—hardly a sign of retreat.

sentences.zh: 王生以火炬喩日，吾亦將借子之矛以刺子之楯焉。

translations.literal: Master Wang used the torch to metaphorize the sun; I too will borrow your spear to pierce your shield.
translations.idiomatic: Wang took a torch for his parable; I will meet spear with shield of his own choosing.

sentences.zh: 把火之人去人轉遠，其光轉微，而日月自出至入，不漸小也。

translations.literal: When the man with the torch goes farther from people, its light becomes progressively fainter; yet from the sun’s emergence to its entry it does not gradually become smaller.
translations.idiomatic: A brand recedes and shrinks; the sun does not dwindle from dawn to dusk.

sentences.zh: 王生以火喩之，謬矣。

translations.literal: Master Wang using fire as metaphor is wrong.
translations.idiomatic: His fire analogy misses the mark.

sentences.zh: 又日之入西方，視之稍稍去，初尚有半，如橫破鏡之狀，須臾淪沒矣。

translations.literal: Again, when the sun enters the west, viewed from here it gradually departs; at first there is still a half, like the shape of a mirror broken horizontally; in a moment it sinks away.
translations.idiomatic: At western set the sun narrows to a half-disk like a mirror snapped crosswise, then slips under in an instant.

sentences.zh: 若如王生之言，日轉北去有半者，其北都沒之頃，宜先如豎破鏡之狀，不應如橫破鏡也。

translations.literal: If it were as Master Wang says, that the sun turns northward and there is a half, then in the moment when its northern side is entirely gone, it ought first to resemble a mirror broken vertically, and ought not resemble a mirror broken horizontally.
translations.idiomatic: On Wang’s mill theory a half-phase should stand upright like a mirror split lengthwise, not lie flat as we see.

sentences.zh: 如此言之，日入西方，不亦孤-{於}-乎？

translations.literal: Stated in this way, the sun’s entering the west—is it not strained?
translations.idiomatic: Argued thus, his picture of a western sunset strains credulity.

sentences.zh: 又月之光微，不及日遠矣。

translations.literal: Again, the moon’s light is faint, far inferior to the sun’s.
translations.idiomatic: Moonlight is pale beside daylight.

sentences.zh: 月盛之時，雖有重-{雲}-敝之，不見月體，而夕猶朗然，是光猶從-{雲}-中而照外也。

translations.literal: When the moon is full, though layered clouds cover it and the moon’s body is not seen, the evening is still bright—therefore light still passes through the clouds to shine outward.
translations.idiomatic: Even on a hazy full moon night the sky stays bright—glow leaks through the veil.

sentences.zh: 日若繞西及北者，其光故應如月在-{雲}-中之狀，不得夜便大暗也。

translations.literal: If the sun were to circle west and north, its light ought therefore to be like the moon’s state inside clouds, and ought not to make the night suddenly very dark.
translations.idiomatic: If the sun circled north through cloud, nights should look like a veiled moon, not pitch black.

sentences.zh: 又日入則星月出焉。

translations.literal: Again, when the sun enters, the stars and moon emerge.
translations.idiomatic: When the sun sets, moon and stars step forth.

sentences.zh: 明知天以日月分主晝夜，相代而照也。

translations.literal: This clearly knows that Heaven uses the sun and moon to divide mastery of day and night, replacing one another in illumination.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven allots day to the sun and night to the moon, each lighting its watch.

sentences.zh: 若日常出者，不應日亦入而星月亦出也。

translations.literal: If the sun were constantly emerging, it ought not be that the sun also enters while stars and moon also emerge.
translations.idiomatic: If the sun never truly set, we would not see stars and moon rise with its fall.

sentences.zh: 又案《河》、《洛》之文，皆-{云}-水火者，陰陽之-{餘}-氣也。

translations.literal: Again, examining the texts of the River Chart and Luo Writings, they all say that water and fire are the surplus qi of yin and yang.
translations.idiomatic: The Hetu and Luoshu treat fire and water as leftover breath of yin and yang.

sentences.zh: 夫言-{餘}-氣，則不能生日月可知也，顧當言日精生火者可耳。

translations.literal: Speaking of surplus qi, then it is knowable that they cannot give birth to the sun and moon; one should rather say that solar essence produces fire.
translations.idiomatic: “Surplus” means they cannot parent the luminaries; one should say solar essence begets fire.

sentences.zh: 若水火是日月所生，則亦何得盡如日月之員乎？

translations.literal: If water and fire were what the sun and moon produced, how could they all be as round as the sun and moon?
translations.idiomatic: If fire and water were born of the two lights, they should be as round as their parents—and they are not.

sentences.zh: 今火出-{於}-陽燧，陽燧員而火不員也；

translations.literal: Now fire comes forth from the yang-sui; the yang-sui is round yet the fire is not round;
translations.idiomatic: Fire struck from a brass burning-mirror is jagged though the mirror is round;

sentences.zh: 水出-{於}-方諸，方諸方而水不方也。

translations.literal: water comes forth from the fangzhu; the fangzhu is square yet the water is not square.
translations.idiomatic: dew coaxed on a square jade is not square though the stone is.

sentences.zh: 又陽燧可以取火-{於}-日，而無取日-{於}-火之理，此則日精之生火明矣，方諸可以取水-{於}-月，而無取月-{于}-水之道，此則月精之生水了矣。

translations.literal: Again, the yang-sui can draw fire from the sun, yet there is no principle of drawing the sun from fire—thus that solar essence produces fire is clear; the fangzhu can draw water from the moon, yet there is no way of drawing the moon from water—thus that lunar essence produces water is settled.
translations.idiomatic: You can kindle from the sun, not distill the sun from flame; you can bead water from the moon, not squeeze the moon from a puddle—essence flows one way.

sentences.zh: 王生又-{云}-遠故視之員。

translations.literal: Master Wang also said that distance makes them appear round.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Chong also claims distance rounds them.

sentences.zh: 若審然者，月初生之時及既虧之-{後}-，何以視之不員乎？

translations.literal: If that were truly so, at the time when the moon first emerges and after it is already waning, why when viewing it is it not round?
translations.idiomatic: Then a waxing sliver or waning crescent should look round from afar—and they do not.

sentences.zh: 而日食或上或下，從側而起，或如鉤至盡。

translations.literal: And in a solar eclipse it may be above or below, rising from the side, or like a hook until exhausted.
translations.idiomatic: Eclipses bite from top or bottom, from the flank, or gnaw like a hook—never a simple shrink.

sentences.zh: 若遠視見員，不宜見其殘缺左右所起也。

translations.literal: If viewed from afar it appears round, one ought not to see its damage and the left and right from which it arises.
translations.idiomatic: If distance alone rounded it, we would not map the notch’s geometry.

sentences.zh: 此則渾天之理，信而有-{-{徴}-}-矣。

translations.literal: On this the principle of Huntian is trustworthy and has verification.
translations.idiomatic: Here the armillary-sphere account wins clear proof.

sentences.zh: 儀象

translations.literal: Instruments and models.
translations.idiomatic: Armillary instruments

sentences.zh: 《虞書》曰：「在旋璣玉衡，以齊七政。

translations.literal: The Yu Documents says: “He applied the pearl-adorned armillary and the jade traverse to align the seven regulators.”
translations.idiomatic: The Shang shu speaks of the pearl-spangled armillary and jade sight-tube to tune the seven governors.

sentences.zh: 」《考靈曜》-{云}-：「分寸之咎，代天氣生，以-{制}-方員。

translations.literal: ” The Kaolingyao says: “The blame of inches and fractions substitutes for Heaven’s qi in engendering, to regulate square and round.
translations.idiomatic: ” The apocryphal Kaolingyao says: “Minute faults stand in for heaven’s breath, shaping the round and square.”

sentences.zh: 方員以成，參以規矩。

translations.literal: Square and round being completed, combine them with compass and try-square.
translations.idiomatic: Once round and square are fixed, compass and square set the scale.

sentences.zh: 昏明主時，乃命中星觀玉儀之-{遊}-。

translations.literal: Dusk and dawn govern the hours; then he orders the mid-stars observed and contemplates the motion of the jade instrument.”
translations.idiomatic: Dawn and dusk mark the hours; then he reads the culminating stars and tracks the jade armillary’s swing.”

sentences.zh: 」鄭玄謂以玉爲渾儀也。

translations.literal: ” Zheng Xuan explains that it means making the armillary of jade.
translations.idiomatic: ” Zheng Xuan glosses this as a jade armillary sphere.

sentences.zh: 《春秋文曜鉤》-{云}-：「唐堯既位，羲和立渾儀。

translations.literal: The Chunqiu Wenyao gou says: “When Tang Yao had already taken the throne, Xi and He set up the armillary.”
translations.idiomatic: The Chunqiu wenyao gou adds: “Once Yao sat the throne, Xi and He raised the armillary.”

sentences.zh: 」此則儀象之設，其來遠矣。

translations.literal: ” Thus the establishment of instruments and models goes back very far.
translations.idiomatic: ” So calibrated models are an ancient office.

sentences.zh: 綿代相傳，史官禁密，學者不睹，故宣、蓋沸騰。

translations.literal: Stretching across generations it was transmitted in succession; the scribes’ offices were forbidden and secret, so scholars did not see them; therefore Xuanye and Gaitian bubbled in dispute.
translations.idiomatic: Kept close in the astrologers’ bureaus, the tools stayed hidden, which is why wild canopy and void theories flourished among outsiders.

sentences.zh: 暨漢太初，落下閎、鮮-{于}-妄人、耿壽昌等造員儀以考暦度。

translations.literal: Down to Han’s Grand Inception, Luoxia Hong, Xianyu Wangren, Geng Shouchang, and others made round instruments to examine calendar degrees.
translations.idiomatic: At Han’s Grand Inception reform, Luoxia Hong, Xianyu Wangren, and Geng Shouchang cast spherical instruments to test the calendar.

sentences.zh: -{後}-至和帝時，賈逵-{繫}-作，又加黃道。

translations.literal: Later, at the time of Emperor He, Jia Kui again made additions and also added the Yellow Road.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor He, Jia Kui rebuilt the gear and added the ecliptic ring.

sentences.zh: 至順帝時，張衡又-{制}-渾象，具内外規、南北極、黃赤道，列二十四氣、二十八宿中外星官及日月五緯，以漏水轉之-{於}-殿上室内，星中出沒與天相應。

translations.literal: At the time of Emperor Shun, Zhang Heng again made a armillary model, with inner and outer circles, south and north poles, Yellow and Red Roads, setting the twenty-four qi, the twenty-eight lodges, inner and outer star offices, and the sun, moon, and five planets; he turned it with dripping water in the hall and inner chamber, and the stars’ emergence and setting matched Heaven.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor Shun, Zhang Heng cast a full armillary—polar axis, ecliptic and equator, twenty-four seasons, twenty-eight mansions, inner and outer constellations, sun, moon, and five wanderers—driven by clepsydra in the palace until model sky matched real sky.

sentences.zh: 因其關戾，又轉瑞輪蓂莢-{於}-階下，隨月虚盈，依暦開落。

translations.literal: Because of its pivot mechanism, he also turned the auspicious wheel of the calyx-pod calendar plant at the stair base, following the moon’s waxing and waning, opening and falling according to the calendar.
translations.idiomatic: He linked the works to a ritual mimosa wheel on the steps that opened its leaves with the lunar month.

sentences.zh: 其-{後}-陸績亦造渾象。

translations.literal: Thereafter Lu Ji also made an armillary model.
translations.idiomatic: Lu Ji later built another sphere.

sentences.zh: 至呉時，中常侍廬江王蕃善數-{術}-，傳劉洪《-{乾}-象暦》，依其法而-{制}-渾儀，立論考度曰：

translations.literal: By the time of Wu, Palace Attendant Wang Fan of Lujiang was skilled in computational methods, transmitted Liu Hong’s Qianxiang Calendar, and according to its method made an armillary, setting forth a discourse examining measures, saying:
translations.idiomatic: In Wu, the eunuch Wang Fan of Lujiang, versed in numbers and Liu Hong’s Qianxiang li, cast an armillary to that pattern and prefaced it with a technical essay:

sentences.zh: 前儒舊説天地之體，狀如鳥卵，天包地外，猶殼之果黃也；

translations.literal: The former scholars’ old theory is that the bodies of Heaven and Earth are shaped like a bird’s egg, Heaven wrapping Earth without, like the shell’s fruit and yolk;
translations.idiomatic: The old masters said heaven and earth nest like an egg—sky as shell, land as yolk;

sentences.zh: 周旋無端，其形渾渾然，故曰渾天也。

translations.literal: revolving without end, their form hunhunran; therefore it is called Huntian.
translations.idiomatic: turning endlessly in one blurred sphere—hence the name “armillary heaven.”

sentences.zh: 周天三百六十五度五百八十九分度之百四十五，半覆地上，半在地下。

translations.literal: The round of Heaven is three hundred sixty-five degrees and one hundred forty-five parts of five hundred eighty-ninths of a degree; half covers the ground above, half is below the ground.
translations.idiomatic: The full circle is 365 145/589 degrees, half above the horizon and half below.

sentences.zh: 其二端謂之南極、北極。

translations.literal: Its two ends are called South Pole and North Pole.
translations.idiomatic: Its axis ends are south and north poles.

sentences.zh: 北極出地三十六度，南極入地三十六度，兩極相去一百八十二度半強。

translations.literal: The north pole emerges thirty-six du above the ground; the south pole enters thirty-six du below the ground; the two poles are one hundred eighty-two and a fraction du apart.
translations.idiomatic: The north pole stands 36° above our plane, the south pole 36° below, the two separated by 182° and a trace.

sentences.zh: 繞北極徑七十二度，常見不隱，謂之上規。

translations.literal: Circling the north pole through seventy-two du, constantly visible and never hidden, is called the upper rule.
translations.idiomatic: The 72° circle about the north pole never sets—the upper circumpolar zone.

sentences.zh: 繞南極七十二度，常隱不見，謂之下規。

translations.literal: Circling the south pole through seventy-two du, constantly hidden and never seen, is called the lower rule.
translations.idiomatic: The matching southern 72° never rises—the lower circumpolar void.

sentences.zh: 赤道帶天之紘，去兩極各九十一度少強。

translations.literal: The Red Road is the girdle-strap of Heaven, ninety-one and a fraction du from each pole.
translations.idiomatic: The equator girdles the sky some ninety-odd degrees from either pole.

sentences.zh: 黃道，日之所行也，半在赤道外，半在赤道内，與赤道東交-{於}-角五少弱，西交-{於}-奎十四少強。

translations.literal: The Yellow Road is the path the sun travels; half is outside the Red Road, half inside; with the Red Road it intersects in the east at Horn at five and a little less, in the west at Bond at fourteen and a little more.
translations.idiomatic: The ecliptic—half north, half south of the equator—cuts the equator east at Horn (5°−) and west at Bond (14°+).

sentences.zh: 其出赤道外極遠者，去赤道二十四度，-{斗}-二十一度是也。

translations.literal: That which emerges farthest outside the Red Road is twenty-four du from the Red Road—Dipper at twenty-one du is the case.
translations.idiomatic: Its greatest northern reach is 24° beyond the equator—winter sun at Dipper 21°.

sentences.zh: 其入赤道内極遠者，亦二十四度，井二十五度是也。

translations.literal: That which enters farthest inside the Red Road is likewise twenty-four du—Well at twenty-five du is the case.
translations.idiomatic: Its deepest southern dip is also 24°—summer sun at Well 25°.

sentences.zh: 日南至在-{斗}-二十一度，去極百一十五度少強。

translations.literal: The sun’s southmost point is at Dipper twenty-one du, one hundred fifteen and a fraction du from the pole.
translations.idiomatic: Winter solstice sits at Dipper 21°, about 115° from the pole.

sentences.zh: 是也日最南，去極最遠，故景最長。

translations.literal: This is the case: the sun is farthest south, farthest from the pole; therefore the shadow is longest.
translations.idiomatic: That is the sun’s southern limit and longest shadow.

sentences.zh: 黃道-{斗}-二十一度，出辰入申，故日亦出辰入申。

translations.literal: The Yellow Road at Dipper twenty-one du emerges in chen and enters in shen; therefore the sun also emerges in chen and enters in shen.
translations.idiomatic: There the ecliptic rises in southeast chen and sets in southwest shen—and so does the sun.

sentences.zh: 日晝行地上百四十六度強，故日短；

translations.literal: The sun by day travels one hundred forty-six and a fraction du above the ground; therefore the day is short;
translations.idiomatic: By day it covers only 146° above us—short daylight;

sentences.zh: 夜行地下二百一十九度少弱，故夜長。

translations.literal: by night it travels two hundred nineteen and a fraction du below the ground; therefore the night is long.
translations.idiomatic: by night it must roll 219° below—long nights.

sentences.zh: 自南至之-{後}-，日去極稍近，故景稍短。

translations.literal: From after the southmost point, the sun goes slightly nearer the pole; therefore the shadow becomes slightly shorter.
translations.idiomatic: After solstice the sun inches north and shadows shorten.

sentences.zh: 日晝行地上度稍多，故日稍長；

translations.literal: The sun by day travels slightly more du above the ground; therefore the day becomes slightly longer;
translations.idiomatic: Day arcs lengthen;

sentences.zh: 夜行地下度稍少，故夜稍短。

translations.literal: by night it travels slightly fewer du below the ground; therefore the night becomes slightly shorter.
translations.idiomatic: night arcs shrink.

sentences.zh: 日所在度稍北，故日稍北，以至-{於}-夏至，日在井二十五度，去極六十七度少強，是日最北，去極最近，景最短。

translations.literal: The du where the sun resides becomes slightly north; therefore the sun becomes slightly north, until at summer solstice the sun is at Well twenty-five du, sixty-seven and a fraction du from the pole—this is the sun farthest north, nearest the pole, shortest shadow.
translations.idiomatic: It climbs until summer solstice at Well 25°, a mere 67° from the pole and the year's shortest gnomon reading.

sentences.zh: 黃道井二十五度，出寅入戌，故日亦出寅入戌。

translations.literal: The Yellow Road at Well twenty-five du emerges in yin and enters in xu; therefore the sun also emerges in yin and enters in xu.
translations.idiomatic: Then the ecliptic rises in northeast yin and sets in northwest xu, and the sun follows.

sentences.zh: 日晝行地上二百一十九度少弱，故日長；

translations.literal: The sun by day travels two hundred nineteen and a fraction du above the ground; therefore the day is long;
translations.idiomatic: Mid-summer daylight spans 219° above—long days;

sentences.zh: 夜行地下百四十六度強，故夜短。

translations.literal: by night it travels one hundred forty-six and a fraction du below the ground; therefore the night is short.
translations.idiomatic: only 146° below—short nights.

sentences.zh: 自夏至之-{後}-，日去極稍遠，故景稍長。

translations.literal: From after summer solstice, the sun goes slightly farther from the pole; therefore the shadow becomes slightly longer.
translations.idiomatic: Past the solstice the sun drifts south again and shadows lengthen.

sentences.zh: 日晝行地上度稍少，故日稍短；

translations.literal: The sun by day travels slightly fewer du above the ground; therefore the day is slightly shorter;
translations.idiomatic: The daylight arc shrinks a notch, so the hours grow a little shorter;

sentences.zh: 夜行地下度稍多，故夜稍長。

translations.literal: by night it travels slightly more du below the ground; therefore the night is slightly longer.
translations.idiomatic: while the night leg underfoot lengthens and the dark hours creep out.

sentences.zh: 日所在度稍南，故日出入稍南，以至-{於}-南至而-{復}-初焉。

translations.literal: The du where the sun resides becomes slightly south; therefore emergence and entry are slightly south, until reaching southmost and again returning to the beginning.
translations.idiomatic: The solar lodge drifts south, taking sunrise and sunset with it, until the southern limit is reached and the cycle begins anew.

sentences.zh: -{斗}-二十一，井二十五，南北相應四十八度。

translations.literal: Dipper twenty-one, Well twenty-five, south and north correspond forty-eight du.
translations.idiomatic: From winter lodge at Dipper 21 to summer lodge at Well 25 spans forty-eight degrees of polar symmetry.

sentences.zh: 春分日在奎十四少強，秋分日在角五少弱，此黃赤二道之交中也。

translations.literal: At spring equinox the sun is at Bond fourteen and a little more; at autumn equinox at Horn five and a little less—this is the crossing of the Yellow and Red Roads.
translations.idiomatic: Spring equinox finds the sun at Bond 14+; autumn equinox at Horn 5−—the two moments when ecliptic and equator cross.

sentences.zh: 去極倶九十一度少強。

translations.literal: From the pole both are ninety-one du and a fraction.
translations.idiomatic: Each lies a fraction over ninety-one degrees from the celestial pole.

sentences.zh: 南北處-{斗}-二十一，井二十五之中，故景居二至長短之中。

translations.literal: South and north lie midway within Dipper twenty-one and Well twenty-five; therefore the shadow sits midway between the two extremes’ lengths.
translations.idiomatic: Equinox sits halfway between the solstice lodges, so the gnomon shadow splits the gap between longest winter shade and shortest summer shade.

sentences.zh: 奎十四，角五，出卯入酉，故日亦出卯入酉。

translations.literal: Bond fourteen, Horn five, emerge mao and enter you; therefore the sun also emerges mao and enters you.
translations.idiomatic: Those points rise in east mao and set in west you, and the sun follows suit on the equinoxes.

sentences.zh: 日晝行地上，夜行地下，倶百八十二度半強，故日見之漏五十刻，不見之漏五十刻，謂之晝夜同。

translations.literal: The sun by day travels above the ground, by night below the ground, both one hundred eighty-two du and a fraction; therefore visible clepsydra fifty marks, invisible fifty marks—called day and night equal.
translations.idiomatic: Each half of the circuit is a little over 182°, so raw day and night clepsydra counts balance at fifty marks apiece.

sentences.zh: 夫天之晝夜以日出沒爲分，人之晝夜以昏明爲限。

translations.literal: Now Heaven’s day and night take sun emergence and setting as division; mankind’s day and night take dusk and dawn as limit.
translations.idiomatic: Astronomy cuts the day at true rise and set; civil time stretches daylight with dawn and dusk.

sentences.zh: 日未出二刻半而明，日入二刻半而昏，故損夜五刻以益晝，是以春秋分漏晝五十五刻。

translations.literal: Two and a half marks before the sun has not yet risen there is light; two and a half marks after sun entry there is still dusk; therefore subtract five night marks to add to day; hence at spring and autumn equinox clepsydra day is fifty-five marks.
translations.idiomatic: Twilight borrows two and a half marks before sunrise and after sunset, shifting five marks from night to day, so the equinox “day” runs fifty-five clepsydra divisions.

sentences.zh: 三光之行，不必有常，-{術}-家以算求之，各有同異，故諸家暦法參差不齊。

translations.literal: The motion of the three luminaries need not be constant; technicalists seek them by calculation, each alike yet different; therefore the calendrical methods of the various schools are uneven.
translations.idiomatic: Sun, moon, and stars keep no single fixed pace; each school computes them differently, which is why calendars disagree.

sentences.zh: 《洛書甄曜度》、《春秋考異郵》皆-{云}-：「周天一百七萬一千-{里}-，一度爲二千九百三十二-{里}-七十一歩二尺七寸四分四百八十七分分之三百六十二。

translations.literal: The Luo shu Zhenyao du and Chunqiu Kaoyi you both say: “Heaven’s circumference is one million seventy-one thousand li; one du is two thousand nine hundred thirty-two li seventy-one bu two chi seven cun and three hundred sixty-two four-hundred eighty-sevenths of a fen.”
translations.idiomatic: Apocryphal texts peg the sky’s rim at 1,071,000 li and each degree at roughly 2,932 li with an elaborate fractional remainder.

sentences.zh: 」陸績-{云}-：「天東西南北徑三十五萬七千-{里}-。

translations.literal: ” Lu Ji said: “Heaven’s east-west-south-north diameter is three hundred fifty-seven thousand li.”
translations.idiomatic: ” Lu Ji rounds the celestial diameter to 357,000 li.

sentences.zh: 」此言周三徑一也。

translations.literal: ” This statement is “circumference three, diameter one.”
translations.idiomatic: ” That is the old π ≈ 3 shortcut.

sentences.zh: 考之徑一不啻周三，率周百四十二而徑四十五，則天徑三十二萬九千四百一-{里}-一百二十二歩二尺二寸一分七十一分分之十。

translations.literal: Examining it, diameter one is not merely circumference three; taking rate circumference one hundred forty-two and diameter forty-five, then Heaven’s diameter is three hundred twenty-nine thousand four hundred one li one hundred twenty-two bu two chi two cun and ten seventy-firsts of a fen.
translations.idiomatic: Closer ratio 142:45 yields a celestial diameter of about 329,401 li with a long fractional tail.

sentences.zh: 《周禮》：「日至之景尺有五寸，謂之地中。

translations.literal: The Rites of Zhou: “The solstice shadow of one chi five cun is called the center of the earth.”
translations.idiomatic: The Zhou li says a summer solstice shadow of one foot five inches marks “earth’s middle.”

sentences.zh: 」鄭衆説：「土圭之長尺有五寸，以夏至之日立八尺之表，其景與土圭等，謂之地中，今潁川陽城地也。

translations.literal: ” Zheng Zhong’s explanation: “The earth-gnomon’s length is one chi five cun; on the summer solstice day erect an eight-chi gnomon; when its shadow equals the earth-gnomon, that is called the center of the earth—now the land of Yangcheng in Yingchuan.”
translations.idiomatic: Zheng Zhong explains: match a 1.5-foot template to an eight-foot pole at summer solstice and you have the central meridian—today’s Yangcheng in Henan.

sentences.zh: 」鄭玄-{云}-：「凡日景-{於}-地，千-{里}-而差一寸，景尺有五寸者，南戴日下萬五千-{里}-也。

translations.literal: ” Zheng Xuan said: “Generally for sun shadows on the ground, each thousand li differs one cun; a shadow of one chi five cun means fifteen thousand li south bears directly under the sun.”
translations.idiomatic: Zheng Xuan adds the rule of one cun per thousand li, so a 1.5-foot shadow implies the subsolar point lies 15,000 li due south.

sentences.zh: 」以此推之，日當去其下地八萬-{里}-矣。

translations.literal: ” From this deducing, the sun ought to be eighty thousand li from the ground beneath it.
translations.idiomatic: From that geometry the sun stands about 80,000 li above the ground below.

sentences.zh: 日邪射陽城，則天徑之半也。

translations.literal: The sun’s diagonal sight-line to Yangcheng is then half Heaven’s diameter.
translations.idiomatic: The oblique ray from sun to Yangcheng equals half the sky’s diameter.

sentences.zh: 天體員如彈丸，地處天之半，而陽城爲中，則日春秋冬夏，昏明晝夜，去陽城皆等，無盈縮矣。

translations.literal: The celestial body is round like a pellet; earth sits at Heaven’s half, and Yangcheng is at the center; then for the sun in spring, summer, autumn, and winter, dusk, dawn, day, and night, distance from Yangcheng is all equal, without surplus or shrinkage.
translations.idiomatic: If heaven is a ball with earth at mid-layer and Yangcheng at the hub, every season’s light and dark should strike Yangcheng evenly—which they do not, unless the slant ray is half the diameter.

sentences.zh: 故知從日邪射陽城，爲天徑之半也。

translations.literal: Therefore one knows that following the sun’s diagonal sight-line to Yangcheng is half Heaven’s diameter.
translations.idiomatic: Hence the sight-line from zenith to Yangcheng really does measure half the celestial span.

sentences.zh: 以句股法言之，旁萬五千-{里}-，句也；

translations.literal: Speaking by gou-gu method, fifteen thousand li to the side is the gou;
translations.idiomatic: In right-triangle terms the 15,000-li horizontal leg is the base;

sentences.zh: 立八萬-{里}-，股也；

translations.literal: erect eighty thousand li, that is the gu;
translations.idiomatic: the 80,000-li vertical is the upright;

sentences.zh: 從日邪射陽城，絃也。

translations.literal: from the sun diagonally sighting Yangcheng is the xian.
translations.idiomatic: and the sun’s slant to Yangcheng is the hypotenuse.

sentences.zh: 以句股求絃法入之，得八萬一千三百九十四-{里}-三十歩五尺三寸六分，天徑之半而地上去天之數也。

translations.literal: Applying the gou-gu method for seeking the xian, one obtains eighty-one thousand three hundred ninety-four li thirty bu five chi three cun six fen—half Heaven’s diameter and the number from the ground up to Heaven.
translations.idiomatic: Pythagoras gives roughly 81,394 li from ground to sky along that ray—half the diameter.

sentences.zh: 倍之，得十六萬二千七百八十八-{里}-六十一歩四尺七寸二分，天徑之數也。

translations.literal: Doubling it, one obtains one hundred sixty-two thousand seven hundred eighty-eight li sixty-one bu four chi seven fen two fen—Heaven’s diameter.
translations.idiomatic: Double it for a full diameter of about 162,788 li.

sentences.zh: 以周率乘之，徑率約之，得五十一萬三千六百八十七-{里}-六十八歩一尺八寸二分，周天之數也。

translations.literal: Multiplying by the circumference rate and reducing by the diameter rate, one obtains five hundred thirteen thousand six hundred eighty-seven li sixty-eight bu one chi eight fen two fen—Heaven’s circumference.
translations.idiomatic: Scale by π to reach a circumference near 513,687 li.

sentences.zh: 減《甄曜度》、《考異郵》五十五萬七千三百一十七-{里}-有奇。

translations.literal: Subtracting from the Zhenyao du and Kaoyi you five hundred fifty-seven thousand three hundred seventeen li and odd.
translations.idiomatic: That falls more than 557,000 li short of the apocryphal totals.

sentences.zh: 一度凡千四百六-{里}-百二十四歩六寸四分十萬七千五百六十五分分之萬九千四十九，減舊度千五百二十五-{里}-二百五十六歩三尺三寸二十一萬五千一百三十分分之十六萬七百三十。

translations.literal: Each du on average is one thousand four hundred six li one hundred twenty-four bu six cun four fen and nineteen thousand forty-nine out of one hundred seven thousand five hundred sixty-five ten-thousandths of a fen, subtracting from the old du one thousand five hundred twenty-five li two hundred fifty-six bu three chi three cun and one hundred sixty thousand seven hundred thirty out of two million one hundred fifty-one thousand one hundred thirty ten-thousandths.
translations.idiomatic: Each degree shrinks by intricate fractions compared with the older canon.

sentences.zh: 分黃赤二道，相興交錯，其間相去二十四度。

translations.literal: Dividing Yellow and Red Roads, they intersect and cross; the distance between them is twenty-four du.
translations.idiomatic: Ecliptic and equator tilt twenty-four degrees apart.

sentences.zh: 以兩儀推之，二道倶三百六十五度有奇，是以知天體員如彈丸也。

translations.literal: Pushing with the two models, both roads are three hundred sixty-five du and odd; thereby one knows the celestial body is round like a pellet.
translations.idiomatic: Both rings run more than 365°—another proof the sky is a sphere.

sentences.zh: 而陸績造渾象，其形如鳥卵，然則黃道應長-{於}-赤道矣。

translations.literal: Yet Lu Ji made an armillary model whose shape was like a bird’s egg; then the Yellow Road ought to be longer than the Red Road.
translations.idiomatic: Lu Ji’s ovoid model would make the ecliptic longer than the equator—an awkward mismatch.

sentences.zh: 績-{云}-「天東西南北徑三十五萬七千-{里}-」，然則績亦以天形正員也，而渾象爲鳥卵，則爲自相違背。

translations.literal: Ji said “Heaven’s east-west-south-north diameter is three hundred fifty-seven thousand li”; then Ji also took Heaven’s shape as truly round, yet the armillary model was a bird’s egg—then it contradicts itself.
translations.idiomatic: Lu Ji insists on a perfect 357,000-li sphere yet builds an egg-shaped globe—his premises collide.

sentences.zh: 古舊渾象以二分爲一度，凡周七尺三寸半分。

translations.literal: The old armillary model took two fen as one du; total circumference seven chi three cun and a half fen.
translations.idiomatic: Older spheres used two fen per degree for a ring about seven chi around.

sentences.zh: 張衡更-{制}-，以四分爲一度，凡周一丈四尺六寸一分。

translations.literal: Zhang Heng remade it, taking four fen as one du; total circumference one zhang four chi six cun one fen.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Heng doubled the scale to four fen per degree, making a ring over fourteen chi.

sentences.zh: 蕃以古-{制}-局小，星辰稠穊，衡器傷大，難可轉移，更-{制}-渾象，以三分爲一度，凡周天一丈九寸五分四分分之三也。

translations.literal: Fan held that the old system was cramped and stars dense; Heng’s instrument was too large and hard to turn; he remade the armillary, taking three fen as one du; total circumference of Heaven one zhang nine cun five fen and three-quarters of a fen.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Fan found the old model crowded and Zhang’s unwieldy, so he split the difference at three fen per degree—about 1.09 zhang to the circle.

sentences.zh: 天文經星

translations.literal: Classical fixed stars.
translations.idiomatic: The classical constellations

sentences.zh: 《洪-{範}-傳》曰：「淸而明者，天之體也。

translations.literal: The Hong fan commentary says: “Clear and bright is the body of Heaven.
translations.idiomatic: The Hong fan tradition says: “Lucid brightness is heaven’s proper form.

sentences.zh: 天忽變色，是謂易常。

translations.literal: Heaven suddenly changing color is called altering the constant.
translations.idiomatic: A sky that suddenly discolors means the norm has shifted.

sentences.zh: 天裂，陽不足，是謂臣強。

translations.literal: Heaven splitting means yang is insufficient; it is called ministers strong.
translations.idiomatic: A riven firmament shows weak yang—ministers overpowering their lord.

sentences.zh: 天裂見人，兵起國亡。

translations.literal: Heaven splitting and a person appearing—armies rise and the state perishes.
translations.idiomatic: If the rent shows a human shape, war follows and the dynasty falls.

sentences.zh: 天鳴有聲，至尊憂且驚。

translations.literal: Heaven sounding with noise—the supreme one worries and is startled.
translations.idiomatic: Thunder in a clear sky alarms the sovereign.

sentences.zh: 皆亂國之所生也。」

translations.literal: All are born from a disordered state.”
translations.idiomatic: Such omens spring from a realm already out of joint.”

sentences.zh: 馬續-{云}-：「天文在圖籍昭昭可知者，經星常宿中外官凡一百一十八名，積數七百八十三，皆有州國官宮物類之象。」

translations.literal: Ma Xu said: “What astronomy sets in charts and registers and is plainly knowable: fixed stars and constant lodges, inner and outer offices, in all one hundred eighteen names, accumulated count seven hundred eighty-three, each having images of regions, states, offices, palaces, and thing-kinds.”
translations.idiomatic: Ma Xu lists 118 named constellations—783 stars—each mapped to territories, courts, and emblems.

sentences.zh: 張衡-{云}-：「文曜麗乎天，其動者有七，日月五星是也。

translations.literal: Zhang Heng said: “The patterned radiance adorning Heaven—those that move are seven: sun, moon, and five planets.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Heng writes: “Seven wanderers paint the sky: sun, moon, and the five planets.

sentences.zh: 日者，陽精之宗；

translations.literal: The sun is the ancestor of yang essence;
translations.idiomatic: The sun is lord of yang essence;

sentences.zh: 月者，陰精之宗；

translations.literal: the moon is the ancestor of yin essence;
translations.idiomatic: the moon is lord of yin essence;

sentences.zh: 五星，五行之精。

translations.literal: the five planets are the essences of the Five Phases.
translations.idiomatic: the five planets embody the five phases.

sentences.zh: 衆星列布，體生-{於}-地，精成-{於}-天，列居錯峙，各有攸屬。

translations.literal: The host of stars arrayed, bodies born from earth, essences completed in Heaven, set in rows and staggered peaks, each has its belonging.
translations.idiomatic: Fixed stars take shape below and shine above, each in its station.

sentences.zh: 在野象物，在朝象官，在人象神。

translations.literal: In the wilds they image things; at court they image offices; among people they image spirits.
translations.idiomatic: In the fields they mirror creatures, in the capital offices, among men the gods.

sentences.zh: 其以神差，有五列焉，是爲三十五名。

translations.literal: According to spirit gradation there are five rows; these make thirty-five names.
translations.idiomatic: Grouped by celestial rank they form five belts and thirty-five titles.

sentences.zh: 一居中央，謂之北-{斗}-。

translations.literal: One resides in the center; it is called the Northern Dipper.
translations.idiomatic: One cluster anchors the pivot—the Northern Dipper.

sentences.zh: 四布-{于}-方各七，爲二十八-{舍}-。

translations.literal: Four spread to the quarters, seven each, making twenty-eight lodges.
translations.idiomatic: Four wings of seven mansions each make the twenty-eight lunar lodges.

sentences.zh: 日月運行，暦示吉凶，五緯躔次，用告禍福。

translations.literal: Sun and moon course, calendars display fortune and misfortune; the five planets tread their sequence, used to announce calamity and blessing.
translations.idiomatic: Sun and moon mark the calendar’s weal and woe; the five wanderers spell fortune in their order.

sentences.zh: 中外之官，常明者百有二十四，可名者三百二十，爲星二千五百，微星之數蓋萬有一千五百二十。
